founded.what: The year a merchant of Reims set up the wine company that became Forest-Fourneaux, the house the Taittinger family later bought, by the Union's chronology.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows a large share of its fruit in its own vineyards, buys the rest from growers and makes the wine itself in Reims.

story: Taittinger dates itself from 1734, when a merchant of Reims set up a wine company that became the house of Forest-Fourneaux. In the First World War a young officer of the Taittinger family was stationed at the Château de la Marquetterie, near Épernay, then a command post of the French army, and the place stayed with him. In 1932 the family bought Forest-Fourneaux, by the library and most accounts, and with it came the château, and the house took the family's name. In 1952 it made the first vintage of Comtes de Champagne, a Blanc de Blancs named for the medieval counts of Champagne. Its wines rest in the chalk cellars beneath the Saint-Nicaise hill in Reims, which the house traces to a thirteenth century abbey, and which UNESCO listed with the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars in 2015. In July 2005 the family sold the house, with its parent company, to the American investor Starwood Capital. On 31 May 2006 the Crédit Agricole bank of the north east bought it back, in partnership with a member of the family, and sold shares back to the family in the years that followed.

style.line: Chardonnay leads, unusual for a large house: light and fresh, with white blossom and lemon, a high share of Chardonnay in the non vintage and long, cool ageing in the chalk of Reims.
style.grapes: Chardonnay leads, from the house's own vineyards and growers; Brut Réserve is about two fifths Chardonnay, a third Pinot Noir and a quarter Meunier, from more than forty crus, by the house.
style.reserve: About three tenths of Brut Réserve is wine of earlier harvests, by the house's own pages.
style.lees: Ten years in the chalk cellars of Saint-Nicaise for Comtes de Champagne, by the house.
style.dosage: 9 grams a litre for Comtes de Champagne 2013 by two importers' sheets, and for the rosé of 2013 by the house.

nv.name: Brut Réserve
nv.note: The non vintage Brut most guests know, sold in some markets as La Française: about two fifths Chardonnay, an unusually high share, by the house.

cuvee.name: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs

first.what: The first vintage, by the house: the year the cuvée was created.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in years the house declares since 1952. The house called the 2009 the thirty second vintage, and its pages have counted thirty seven and forty two at later dates.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay alone, from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.
cuvee.sites: Five Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, by the house: Avize, Cramant, Chouilly, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Oger.
cuvee.making: Made from the first pressing alone, with about a twentieth of the wine aged three to four months in oak casks, a third of them renewed each year, by two importers' sheets, and the rest kept in vats. The bottles then rest for ten years in the chalk cellars beneath the Saint-Nicaise hill, by the house, and the 2013 was dosed at 9 grams a litre.
cuvee.lees: Ten years in the chalk cellars of Saint-Nicaise before release, by the house.
cuvee.bottle: The bottle carries the seal of a thirteenth century count of Champagne, by the house, the image that gives the cuvée its name.
cuvee.young: Ripe lemon and white peach over pastry and brioche, with a chalky line and a finish of ginger and liquorice, by the house's own note.
cuvee.aged: With age it turns to pastry, toasted nuts and ripe yellow apple, by one vertical tasting, and gains an inner richness one critic likens to a liqueur.

forms.name: Comtes de Champagne Rosé
forms.note: The rosé of the same name, a different wine: Grand Cru Pinot Noir leads, three fifths to seven tenths by the house's sheets, with Chardonnay and some red wine of Bouzy.

cuvee.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold: the house gives 11 for the 2013; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Taittinger dates itself from 1734, when a Reims merchant founded the firm the family bought in 1932. A young Taittinger officer had been stationed nearby in the First World War and fell for the château that came with it. Its wines age in chalk cellars beneath the Saint-Nicaise hill, part of the UNESCO listing of 2015. The style is led by Chardonnay, unusual for a large house, so it reads fresh, with white blossom and lemon. Guests often ask for its Brut Réserve. Its prestige cuvée, Comtes de Champagne, is a vintage Blanc de Blancs first made in 1952.
table.house10: Taittinger is the Reims house the family bought in 1932, Chardonnay led and fresh, aged in chalk cellars beneath the city.
table.cuvee45: Comtes de Champagne is Taittinger's vintage Blanc de Blancs, first made in 1952. It is Chardonnay alone from five Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, among them Avize and Le Mesnil. A small part of the wine is aged in oak, and the bottles rest ten years in chalk cellars under Reims. The name honours the medieval counts of Champagne, whose seal is on the bottle. Ripe lemon, white peach and brioche end on a note of ginger. Cool rather than cold, in a white wine glass, is how I serve it.
table.sale: Comtes de Champagne is Grand Cru Chardonnay alone, aged ten years in chalk cellars beneath Reims. May I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Comtes de Champagne is Taittinger's vintage Blanc de Blancs, Grand Cru Chardonnay of the Côte des Blancs, first made in 1952.
table.cuvee20: Taittinger draws Comtes de Champagne from five Grand Cru villages, Chardonnay alone, as a vintage wine. It rests ten years in chalk cellars under Reims and gives ripe lemon, white peach and brioche.

guests.q: Who were the Comtes de Champagne?
guests.a: The medieval counts who ruled Champagne. The house named its Blanc de Blancs for them, and the bottle carries the seal of one of them, a count of the thirteenth century.

guests.q: Is the Comtes de Champagne Rosé the same wine in pink?
guests.a: No. The rosé is led by Grand Cru Pinot Noir, three fifths to seven tenths by the house's sheets, with Chardonnay for the rest; the white Comtes is Chardonnay alone.
The family bought it in 1932, sold it in 2005, and from 2006 bought shares back with a regional bank's backing, so the family's name and hand returned.

traps: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay; the Rose of the same name is Pinot-led.
The class sheet prints Comtes de Chamoagne, a slip of the keys; the label reads Comtes de Champagne.
Comtes de Champagne is Taittinger's Blanc de Blancs, of Reims; Dom Ruinart is Ruinart's, and Le Mesnil is Salon's.
Taittinger dates itself from 1734 as Forest-Fourneaux; the family's name is on the house only from 1932.

sheet.label: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs
sheet.note: The sheet types Chamoagne for Champagne, an o where the p should be. The label reads Comtes de Champagne, the counts of Champagne, with Blanc de Blancs and the vintage, and newer bottles add Grands Crus.

cards.front: Taittinger: name its prestige cuvée on the class sheet, and the grape it is made from.
cards.back: Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs: Chardonnay alone, from five Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.

Comtes de Champagne: how long do the bottles rest in the chalk cellars before release?
cards.back: Ten years, beneath the Saint-Nicaise hill in Reims, by the house.

questions.q: A guest asks for the vintage Blanc de Blancs named for the medieval counts of the region. Which house makes it?
questions.exp: Comtes de Champagne is Taittinger's Blanc de Blancs, first made in 1952. Ruinart's Blanc de Blancs prestige cuvée is Dom Ruinart, Salon's is Le Mesnil and Delamotte, its sister house, makes a Blanc de Blancs of its own.

questions.q: In which year did the Taittinger family buy the house of Forest-Fourneaux?
questions.exp: The family bought Forest-Fourneaux in 1932 by most accounts. 1734 is the year the house dates itself from, 1952 the first vintage of Comtes de Champagne and 2006 the year a regional bank and the family bought it back.

questions.q: Which grape leads Comtes de Champagne Rosé, unlike the white Comtes?
questions.exp: The rosé is three fifths to seven tenths Grand Cru Pinot Noir of the Montagne de Reims by the house's sheets, with Chardonnay for the rest. The white Comtes de Champagne is Chardonnay alone, and Meunier is in Brut Réserve, not in either Comtes.

report: Built on the library's p-taittinger and w-comtes-de-champagne, contradicting neither; the library trap on the rosé is kept word for word, Rose and Pinot-led as it prints them, and the founding year 1734 is the library's.

The family's purchase: 1932 by the library and Wikipedia, while the Union's chronology says Forest-Fourneaux became the Taittinger house in 1931; the château is dated 1932 by the house and 1934 by a Union article. The record follows 1932 and the refuter should settle it.

Nobody is named: the merchant of 1734 and the officer of the First World War are described, their dates not sought; the counts of Champagne are described, and the thirteenth century count whose seal is on the bottle is not named because his dates were not confirmed in two sources.

The sale of July 2005 to Starwood Capital and the purchase of 31 May 2006 by the Crédit Agricole bank of the north east rest on Wikipedia, Decanter and the trade press; the shares the family later regained, given as 37 or 41 per cent by account, are left out.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label by the author; the refuter read NM 162 001 on a Brut label in the Open Food Facts database.

Style fields: vessels and malolactic are empty, no house page read stating them; the oak share of Comtes, about one twentieth for three to four months, is two importers', who say a third of the casks are renewed each year, so the record no longer calls them new. One critic says Comtes goes through malolactic conversion, left out on one source.
The dosage of 9 grams a litre for Comtes 2013 rests on two importers' sheets; the house's own sheet for the white was not read, only the rosé's.
The vintage count moves by page: thirty two for the 2009 by the house's press kit, thirty seven and forty two on later pages, so the record gives no single number.
Comtes de Champagne Rosé's first vintage was not found and is left out; the plan's thought of a 1966 was not confirmed.
The Saint-Nicaise cellars traced to a thirteenth century abbey is the house's account; the house's Chardonnay legend of the Holy Land is left out.

The young glass is the house's note on the 2013 with the library's white peach and brioche; the aged glass rests on one vertical report, whose mature orchard fruit the record names as ripe yellow apple, and one critic.
